title: Malaysia reopens to Bangladeshi workers: 10,000 jobs, 338 agencies and a Tk 8,000 medical fee
excerpt: The government says the first 10,000 places are free of charge to workers, but the full cost of migrating has not been published.
content:
Recruitment of Bangladeshi workers to Malaysia has restarted after a long pause, the Ministry of Expatriates’ Welfare and Overseas Employment announced on 15 October. Malaysia has agreed in principle to take 10,000 Bangladeshi workers “at no cost” to them, at Bangladesh’s request, Prothom Alo reported.

How the process works

  • Agencies: Malaysia has listed 338 Bangladeshi recruiting agencies: the state-run BOESL, 25 private processing agencies and 312 others. The earlier list had 423.
  • Steps: agencies collect demand letters from Malaysian employers, recruit workers under Bangladeshi rules, process visas with Malaysian authorities through BOESL and the 25 processing agencies, and then get BMET clearance.
  • Medical tests began on 31 October at approved centres only. The fee is fixed at Tk 8,000, bdnews24.com reported. Tests done before 31 October are not accepted. The Daily Star reported on 7 November that Malaysia has listed 51 approved medical centres.
  • Agreement: the process runs under the Bangladesh-Malaysia memorandum of understanding signed on 18 December 2022.

Warnings to workers

The ministry has warned workers not to hand passports or money to anyone without checking that they are approved, saying brokers have already tried to collect them. Workers can report overcharging, harassment or delays to the ministry at secretary@probashi.gov.bd. Centres or agencies found breaking the rules can be closed or suspended.

The government has not published the total cost of migrating to Malaysia, so it is not yet clear what workers will pay beyond the medical fee.

Why it matters

Malaysia has long been one of the most expensive and abuse-prone routes for Bangladeshi workers, and earlier recruitment rounds ended in allegations of a syndicate, inflated fees and stranded workers. Migration NGOs, legal aid groups and union-level migration information centres can help workers check approved agencies and centres, keep receipts, and report overcharging early.

What to watch

Publication of the full cost structure, whether workers are charged beyond the medical fee, and whether Malaysia raises the 10,000 quota.
